stem: A nurse notices that two different medications have very similar container labels and packaging. No error has occurred yet. What is the best action?

options.A: Ignore the similarity until a wrong-drug event actually occurs.
options.B: Report the look-alike packaging as a medication-error hazard through the appropriate safety process.
options.C: Assume the packaging is safe because both products are FDA approved.
options.D: Rely only on memory to distinguish the products during administration.

rationale: FDA identifies look-alike container labels as a preventable medication-error hazard and encourages reporting of medication errors and circumstances that may cause or lead to an error, including look-alike labels. A safety concern should therefore be reported before harm occurs. B is correct.
educational_objective: Recognize and report look-alike drug labeling or packaging as a preventable medication-safety hazard before an error occurs.
source_document_title: Medication Errors Related to CDER-Regulated Drug Products
source_locator: Medication-error definition/examples; postapproval monitoring and reporting — look-alike container labels
source_claim_supported: Look-alike container labels can cause preventable wrong-drug errors, and FDA encourages reporting of circumstances such as look-alike labels that may cause or lead to medication errors.
blueprint_locator: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — medication-error prevention and reporting
correction_summary: Replaced the vague ISMP resource citation with current FDA medication-error guidance and narrowed the item to the directly supported nursing action: recognize and report the look-alike packaging hazard before an error occurs. Reduced difficulty from hard to easy.
audit_findings: FDA directly identifies look-alike container labels as preventable error hazards and encourages reporting before harm. B is uniquely correct; independent second pass found no unresolved ambiguity.
